Synchronous Phasors and the Power Angle (Ch8)

Why this matters in the exam: Q4 of every paper is Ch8 plus per-unit. After the per-unit set-up in Q4a (pack M10), Q4b is a phasor or power-angle calculation. Jun24 Q4b (6 marks) asks for , and for a generator at 0.9 leading pf, and is almost the same as Practice Question 8.8. Jun23 Q4b (7 marks) is plant power-factor correction with a synchronous motor, the same method as 8.14 and 8.15. Q4c (8–9 marks) is always words-only short answers. So about 15 of the 20 Q4 marks use this pack. Ch8 has no worked solutions in the course files, only numerical answers, so every solution below has been rebuilt and checked against those answers.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The equivalent circuit and the one phasor equation (Lecture 8.4.2)

The course models a round-rotor synchronous machine, per phase, as an induced voltage behind the synchronous impedance . The current is drawn flowing out of the machine to the terminals (generator convention):

Symbol Meaning Notes
terminal (phase) voltage the reference phasor:
stator current, out of the machine , where
open-circuit (excitation) voltage its size is set by the field current
rotor angle = angle of relative to generating, motoring
synchronous reactance about 10 times , so is highly inductive
  • When to use it: whenever you are given terminal conditions (, and with pf, or with ) and asked for the excitation , the field current , or the rotor angle .
  • Trap: the sign of the current angle. Lagging means is behind : is negative. Leading means is positive. Getting this wrong flips the whole answer (for example 2.41 pu instead of 1.634 pu in Jun24 Q4b).

The phasor diagram (generator convention, R neglected). Draw along the real axis. Draw at angle . Then is long and points 90° ahead of . It starts at the tip of . runs from the origin to its tip.

Output pf (generator) Current points Result Excitation
Lagging below up and to the right long, small over-excited,
Unity along straight up “normal” excitation
Leading above up and to the left short, large under-excited,

Set up for Jun24 Q4b: the operating point sits just below the 90° peak of the P–δ curve. Raise E0 and watch δ fall and the current swing from leading to lagging.

1.2 Motor convention (Lecture 8.2.2, 8.4.6)

The course defines motoring by the rotor angle: in a motor the stator field leads the rotor, so . The course does not use a separate motor equation. You have two equivalent ways to handle a motor:

  1. Course way: keep , but use the generator-convention current, which is the input current reversed: . The answer comes out with negative.
  2. Motor convention: take as the current into the machine. Then , so .

Both give exactly the same . For a motor, “leading pf” means the input current leads .

Input pf (motor) Excitation Reactive power
Lagging under-excited motor absorbs Q (like an induction motor)
Unity normal Q = 0
Leading over-excited motor supplies Q to the plant (this is power-factor correction)

One rule that covers both modes: an over-excited synchronous machine generates Q. An under-excited one absorbs Q.

1.3 Q sign convention (formula sheet: )

The course uses . A lagging current () gives . For a load or motor (current in), means it absorbs Q. For a generator (current out), a lagging output current means the generator is delivering Q to the system. Jun23 Q4a confirms this: P = 100 MW and Q = +50 MVAr gives pu.

1.5 Stability limit (Lecture 8.2.2, 8.4.5, 8.4.7)

  • : no load, P = 0.
  • : theoretical stability limit (pull-out). Beyond it, more mechanical input gives less electrical output, so the rotor accelerates away and loses synchronism.
  • Rated torque is at about (Lecture 8.2.2). About is the typical largest operating value, which leaves a safety margin (Lecture 8.4.5).
  • Losing synchronism causes very large fault currents and oscillating torques, and can damage the generator and turbine (spring-and-disks analogy, 8.4.7).
  • Lower excitation means a lower . At the same P, an under-excited (leading) generator runs at a larger , closer to the limit. That is why the excitation must “not be reduced so far that gets close to 90°” (Lecture 8.6.2).

1.6 Two operating controls (Lecture 8.5.1, 8.6.2–8.6.3)

Control Sets How
Mechanical input (steam valve) real power P, and so
Field current (excitation) , and so Q and pf at constant P, is fixed, so the tip of moves along a vertical line

Excitation to field current. On the linear (air-gap) line, , so . is the field current that gives rated voltage on open circuit (the synchronising value, PQ 8.10c).

N3 (a): lagging at E0 = 2.0 pu, δ = 33°. Lower E0 to about 1.14 pu while raising δ to about 73° to hold P = 0.68 pu: the current turns leading and P_max falls.

1.7 V-curves (Lecture 8.6.4)

At constant P, plot stator current against . The curve is a “V”:

  • The minimum is at unity pf (Q = 0), where .
  • Moving away from that point either way adds |Q|, so grows and grows.
  • Higher (over-excited): the machine generates Q. Lower (under-excited): it absorbs Q.
  • A pf-versus- curve is an inverted V with its peak (pf = 1) at the same .
  • A larger P moves the whole V up and to the right.

Careful with labels. Slide 8.6.4 labels the high- side “leading pf”. That is the pf seen from the supply (the input or motor view). For a generator’s output current, the high- side is lagging (Slide 8.6.3 diagram). In the exam, say “generates Q” or “absorbs Q”. Those words are unambiguous.

1.8 Capability and power-factor correction (Lecture 8.6.5–8.6.7)

The stator VA rating limits a synchronous machine, because of stator winding heating. At input power :

  • A synchronous motor’s electrical input is . Use , not , in the triangle (PQ 8.13: 270 kW/0.92 = 293.5 kW).
  • Over-excited, the motor supplies (negative in the course convention, because the input current leads).
  • Synchronous compensator: a machine run with P = 0. It can generate or absorb Q up to its full VA rating.
  • Plant pf: add all the P values, add all the Q values (lagging +, leading −), and then .

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Wrong sign on the current angle. Leading means pf. In Jun24 Q4b, using −25.84° gives pu instead of 1.634 pu.
  • Using P instead of S for |I|. . “Rated volt-amp output” means S = 1 pu, not P = 1 pu.
  • Recomputing for . “Excitation fixed at the above level” means you keep the old and just set (PQ 8.8c, Jun24 Q4b(iii)).
  • Forgetting that Jun24 Q4b(iii) asks for the angle as well. The answer is “δ = 90°” plus . That is the second mark.
  • Factor-of-3 errors in SI power. Phase voltages: multiply by 3. Line voltages: do not.
  • Using the mechanical power in the capability triangle. Use for both the induction motor and the synchronous motor.
  • Over- and under-excitation the wrong way round for motors. An over-excited machine always generates Q. For a generator that is a lagging output. For a motor it is a leading input.
  • No “lag” or “lead” on the final pf. Jun23 Q4b(iii) expects “0.9955 lag”.

Jun23 Q4c (past exam, 8 marks). 4c) Short-Answer Questions [ 8 marks ] Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without using any sketches, drawings or equations).

i) Explain the concept of power-factor correction. Why is power-factor correction useful in power systems? [ 3 marks ]

ii) Carefully explain the differences and similarities between transformers and induction machines. [ 3 marks ]

iii) Consider a squirrel-cage induction machine. If the rotor cage was made from a perfect conductor (with infinite conductivity) how would this affect the properties of the machine? [ 2 marks ]

Model answers

These are built from the answer sheets’ points. The sheet says you do not need every point for full marks. Aim for about one solid point per mark.

(i) Power-factor correction [3]

  • Many loads, such as induction motors, draw reactive power as well as real power. Their current lags the voltage.
  • Reactive power is energy oscillating back and forth between the source and the load. It does no useful work, but it adds to the current.
  • The extra current loads up generators, transformers and cables, causes extra resistive losses and voltage drop, and raises the VA demand that the supply company charges for.
  • Correction means supplying the reactive power locally. Capacitors, or an over-excited synchronous motor, are connected in parallel with the load and generate reactive power. The supply then provides mostly real power, and the pf moves towards unity.
  • The useful result: lower current and losses for the same useful power, freed-up capacity, and lower tariffs.

(ii) Transformers vs induction machines [3]

  • Similarities: both can run from three-phase AC, have primary (stator) and secondary (rotor) windings on a magnetic core, and transfer power by mutual induction. Their equivalent circuits have the same form: winding resistances, leakage reactances, a magnetising reactance and a core-loss resistance.
  • Differences: the induction machine’s secondary is a rotating, short-circuited winding. Its rotor frequency is the slip frequency, not the stator frequency. It has an air gap, so its magnetising current is much larger.
  • In the induction-machine equivalent circuit, the referred rotor resistance is divided by the slip. That term represents the mechanical output plus the rotor loss.

(iii) Perfectly conducting rotor cage [2]

  • The referred rotor resistance would be zero.
  • The torque–speed curve would be vertical at synchronous speed, like a synchronous machine. The machine could only produce torque at synchronous speed.
  • There would be no rotor copper losses, so the efficiency would be higher.
  • The starting torque would be zero, so the motor could not start by itself.

Jun24 Q4c (past exam, 9 marks). 4c) Short-Answer Questions [ 9 marks ] Answer the following questions using words only (that is, without using any sketches, drawings or equations).

i) We have discussed three types of electric power: real, reactive and apparent. Explain briefly what each one is and their practical significance. [ 3 marks ]

ii) Consider a transformer operating from an AC supply. Carefully explain what are the main types of losses in the transformer, how are they modelled in the simplified equivalent circuit, and how do these vary with output power. [ 3 marks ]

iii) Carefully explain why the input current of an induction machine under no-load conditions is not zero. What are the physical effects which cause this? [ 3 marks ]

Model answers

These are built from the answer sheets’ points. The sheet says you do not need every point for full marks. Aim for about one solid point per mark.

(i) Real, reactive and apparent power [3]

  • Real power: produced by the part of the current that is in phase with the voltage. It is the average of the instantaneous power, it is energy that flows one way from source to load, and it does useful work. Resistors absorb it.
  • Reactive power: produced by the part of the current that is 90° out of phase with the voltage. Its average is zero, because energy oscillates between source and load each cycle, so it does no useful work. Inductors absorb it and capacitors generate it. It still adds to the current and the losses.
  • Both real and reactive power are scalar quantities.
  • Apparent power: the magnitude of the complex power, whose real part is the real power and whose imaginary part is the reactive power. It is the product of rms voltage and total current, so it sets the current and the ratings (VA) of generators, transformers and cables.

(ii) Transformer losses [3]

  • Copper (winding) loss: resistive heating in the primary and secondary windings. It is modelled by the series winding resistances. It is proportional to current squared, so it rises with the square of the output power.
  • Iron (core) loss: hysteresis and eddy-current loss in the core, caused by the alternating flux. It is modelled by the parallel core-loss resistance. It depends on the voltage and frequency, not the load, so it is roughly constant with output power.

(iii) Why induction-machine no-load current is not zero [3]

  • Magnetising current is needed to set up the rotating air-gap flux. Because there is an air gap, this current is large. It is modelled by the magnetising reactance.
  • Core-loss current supplies the hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the stator and rotor iron. It is modelled by the core-loss resistance.
  • Even at no load, the rotor needs some torque to overcome mechanical losses: bearing friction, and windage (air drag and the cooling fan). So it runs slightly below synchronous speed with a small rotor current. That draws a little real power.
  • So the no-load current is mostly reactive (a low pf), plus a small real component.

Practice Questions, Ch8 short answers (j) and (k) (bonus). From “Some Short-Answer Questions” at the end of Chapter 8:

j) With the aid of sketch, explain what limits the reactive power capability of a synchronous machine.
k) Why is the power-factor of industrial plants usually lagging? Why are synchronous motors sometimes used in such plants?

Model answers
    1. Reactive power capability is limited mainly by the stator VA rating, because of stator winding heating. At a real power P, the most Q available is the square root of (rated S squared minus P squared). At full rated real power, no reactive power is left. When absorbing Q (under-excited), the machine is also limited by the rotor angle approaching the stability limit.
    1. Industrial plant pf is usually lagging, because most loads are induction motors that need magnetising current. Synchronous motors are used because, when over-excited, they draw leading current and supply reactive power. That corrects the plant pf and lowers the VA charges, while also driving a constant-speed load.

6. Quick recall check

  1. At what rotor angle does a round-rotor machine deliver maximum power, and what happens if you try to go past it?

  3. Does the per-unit give per-phase or three-phase power?
  4. A 100 kVA synchronous motor drives 60 kW at 100% efficiency. What is the most leading reactive power it can supply?
  5. On a V-curve at constant P, where is the stator current a minimum, and what is the pf there?
Answers
  1. At (the theoretical stability limit). Past it, the machine loses synchronism (pull-out), with large currents and oscillating torques. In practice it is run at about 75° or less.
  2. Under-excited. It absorbs Q.
  3. Three-phase. Multiply by to get watts.
  4. kVAr, which is −80 kVAr in the course sign convention.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

CH8 PHASORS & POWER ANGLE (rms, per phase, generator convention: I OUT)
E0 = V + I(R + jXs)     V = |V|∠0 ref,  I = (S/V)∠phi
  phi = -acos(pf) LAGGING,  +acos(pf) LEADING        |I| = P/(V*pf)
  delta = angle(E0): >0 generating, <0 motoring
MOTOR: I_in = -I  ->  E0 = V - jXs*I_in   (same answer, delta < 0)
P = (V*E0/Xs) sin(delta)  pu = 3-phase pu (x S_base -> W)
  SI: phase V -> x3 ;  line V (VL*EL/Xs) -> already 3-phase
Pmax = V*E0/Xs at delta = 90 deg (keep OLD E0); practical limit ~75 deg
Q_gen = (V*E0*cos(delta) - V^2)/Xs  [check only; + = delivers Q]
Over-excited -> GENERATES Q (gen: lagging out; motor: leading in)
Under-excited -> ABSORBS Q (gen: leading out, big delta, low Pmax)
I_F = E0(pu) x I_F(E0 = 1 pu);  E0_line = E0(pu) x V_base,L
V-curve (const P): |I| min at pf = 1; either side |I| up (S = sqrt(P^2+Q^2))
CAPABILITY: |Q|max = sqrt(S_rated^2 - P_E^2), P_E = P_M/eta
PFC: sum P, sum Q (lag +, lead -) -> pf = cos(atan(Qtot/Ptot)), state lag/lead
Motor E for PFC: S_m = (P_E + jQ)/S_rated, I_m = conj(S_m/V), E0 = V - jXs*I_m
